---
title: "Agreement"
---

## Building the matrix

Reliability coefficients need one row per unit of analysis and one column per
coder. The fragments export is longer than that, one row per annotation *and*
code, so it has to be reshaped first:

```r
u <- qda_units(frag)
qda_agreement(u)
```

Reshaping forces two decisions. Both are easy to get silently wrong in a
hand-written script, and both change the result in the flattering direction,
so `units()` makes you take them consciously.

### Segments nobody coded

When two coders both leave a segment alone, they agree it is irrelevant. That
is agreement, and leaving it out answers a different, friendlier question:
how well did the coders agree *about the material one of them marked*.

Those segments only enter the matrix if you pass the `uncoded` export:

```r
u <- qda_units(frag, uncoded = qda_read(qda_example("easyqda-uncoded.csv")))
```

Without it they are simply absent. The package will not warn you, because it
cannot tell whether you meant to leave them out, but now you know.

### Segments coded twice by one coder

If a coder put three codes on one segment, there is no single value to compare
against the other coder's one value. Such cells become missing and are counted:

```r
qda_agreement(u)$multi_set_aside
```

Quote that count next to the coefficient. A kappa computed after quietly
dropping a tenth of the material is not the kappa of your study. If multiple
coding is normal in your project, ask about each code separately instead:

```r
b <- qda_units_binary(frag, "Belastung")   # yes/no per segment
qda_kappa(b)
```

A segment carrying three codes then contributes to all three questions rather
than to none.

## Which coefficient

| Function | Coders | Chance is estimated from |
|---|---|---|
| `qda_percent_agreement()` | any | nothing — raw share of agreeing pairs |
| `qda_kappa()` | exactly 2 | the coders' own marginals [@CoefficientAgreement] |
| `qda_brennan()` | exactly 2 | a uniform `1/q` [@Brennan1981CoefficientKappa] — this is what MAXQDA reports |
| `qda_fleiss()` | any | the pooled category distribution |
| `qda_alpha()` | any, gaps allowed | the coincidence matrix [@Krippendorff2004ReliabilityContent] |
| `qda_ac1()` | any | Gwet's correction, stable under skewed marginals |

### The formulas behind them

Every chance-corrected coefficient in the table is the same fraction — how
much of the agreement that chance leaves open was actually achieved:

$$
\kappa \;=\; \frac{P_o - P_e}{1 - P_e}
$$

with

- $P_o$ — the observed share of agreeing pairs,
- $P_e$ — the agreement expected by chance.

The coefficients differ *only* in what they put into $P_e$. Cohen
estimates it from the two coders' own marginal distributions
[@CoefficientAgreement]:

$$
P_e^{\text{Cohen}} \;=\; \sum_{q} p_{1q}\, p_{2q},
$$

with

- $q$ — one category of the code system; the sum runs over all of them,
- $p_{1q}$, $p_{2q}$ — the share of category $q$ in the first and the
  second coder's codings.

Brennan and Prediger replace that with a uniform $1/q$ over the $q$
categories [@Brennan1981CoefficientKappa]. Krippendorff's alpha states the
same idea as a ratio of disagreements, observed over expected, computed from
the coincidence matrix — which is what lets it absorb missing cells and any
number of coders [@Krippendorff2004ReliabilityContent; @Hayes2007AnsweringCall]:

$$
\alpha \;=\; 1 - \frac{D_o}{D_e}.
$$

with

- $D_o$ — the disagreement observed between the coders,
- $D_e$ — the disagreement expected by chance, both computed from the
  coincidence matrix.

`agreement()` reports all of them at once, which is the recommended way to
look at them. They disagree exactly where the marginals are skewed, and that
disagreement is itself the finding:

```r
u <- cbind(ann = c("A", "A", "A", "B"), bob = c("A", "A", "A", "A"))
qda_percent_agreement(u)   # 0.75
qda_kappa(u)               # 0
qda_ac1(u)                 # 0.68
```

The coders disagreed once in four segments and Cohen's kappa reports zero.
Nothing is broken: almost everything is category `A`, so chance alone would
produce that much agreement — $P_e$ swallows $P_o$. This is the kappa
paradox, described and resolved in a classic pair of papers
[@Feinstein1990HighAgreement; @Cicchetti1990HighAgreement], and it is a
property of the measure, not of your coding. Report AC1 beside it, and if
the two diverge, say so rather than picking the friendlier one.

Coefficients that are mathematically undefined come back as `nan`, never as a
convenient number. Cohen's kappa on three coders raises instead of silently
using the first two columns.

## Where in the code system agreement breaks down

A hierarchical code system can be read at several depths. Coders who split
over `Belastung/beruflich` versus `Belastung/privat` still agree the segment
is about `Belastung`. Flattening paths level by level shows where the
agreement is actually lost:

```r
qda_level_agreement(u)
qda_plot_level_agreement(u)
```

A curve that is high at level 1 and collapses at level 3 says the top of your
code system is solid and its leaves are not yet defined sharply enough. That
is a statement about the codebook, not about the coders.

## Which pairs cost you the agreement

```r
qda_confusion(u, only_disagreements = TRUE)
```

Usually a handful of category pairs account for most of the disagreement, and
those are the definitions to work on. This turns a disappointing coefficient
into a list of things to fix.
